blockMcqs.question: What does the BST ordering invariant require at every node?
options: Left child smaller, right child larger, children only
Entire left subtree smaller, entire right subtree larger
Every level fully filled before the next
Heights of the two subtrees differ by at most 1
blockMcqs.explanation: It constrains whole subtrees, not just immediate children — that's why deep violations exist.

blockMcqs.question: How do depth and height of a node differ?
options: Depth counts down to a leaf, height up to root
Depth counts up to root, height down to a leaf
They are always equal in a binary tree
Height counts nodes, depth counts edges
blockMcqs.explanation: They run in opposite directions; the root has depth 0, a leaf has height 0.

blockMcqs.question: Which traversal emits a BST's keys in sorted order?
options: Pre-order
Post-order
In-order
Level-order
blockMcqs.explanation: Left→Node→Right plus the invariant emits smaller keys before larger ones.

blockMcqs.question: What separates pre-, in-, and post-order traversals?
options: They use different data structures
When the node is processed relative to the recursive calls
Their time complexity differs
Only post-order can run iteratively
blockMcqs.explanation: Same DFS recursion; you just move the visit line before, between, or after the calls.

blockMcqs.question: What bounds the cost of a BST search?
options: The number of nodes, n
The tree's height, h
The number of leaves
Always exactly log n
blockMcqs.explanation: Each step descends one level, so a skewed tree of height n costs O(n).

blockMcqs.question: To delete a BST node with two children, you replace it with:
options: Its left child directly
The root of the tree
Its in-order successor
A randomly chosen descendant
blockMcqs.explanation: The next-larger key (leftmost of the right subtree) keeps the ordering intact.

blockMcqs.question: Why does inserting sorted keys into a plain BST hurt?
options: It triggers constant rebalancing rotations
It degenerates into a line of height n, so O(n)
Duplicate keys get rejected
In-order traversal stops being sorted
blockMcqs.explanation: Each key hangs to one side, building a linked list rather than a balanced tree.

blockMcqs.question: When does a red-black tree beat an AVL tree?
options: Read-heavy workloads needing the shallowest tree
Write-heavy workloads, fewer rotations per change
When O(1) lookups are required
When keys must stay unsorted
blockMcqs.explanation: Looser balance means fewer rotations on writes; AVL's strictness favors reads.

blockMcqs.question: Why do databases use B-trees instead of binary BSTs?
options: Binary trees cannot store sorted keys
Wide nodes fit a disk block, making the tree shallow
B-trees avoid all rotations
Binary trees use too much CPU cache
blockMcqs.explanation: Disks read in blocks; many keys per node means ~4 levels and few disk reads.

blockMcqs.question: What's the correct way to validate a BST?
options: Compare each node only against its two children
Carry a (min, max) range, or check in-order is increasing
Confirm the tree height is log n
Count nodes on left and right sides
blockMcqs.explanation: Local checks miss grandparent violations; a range or sorted scan catches them.

blockMcqs.question: Where is a node's in-order successor actually found?
options: It is always the node's right child
The leftmost node of the right subtree
The rightmost node of the left subtree
The parent of the node
blockMcqs.explanation: Go right once, then left as far as possible; the right child only qualifies if it has no left subtree.
